title: X-Z Round Scheduling for the Surface Code with Defects under Biased Noise
authors: Lakshika Rathi, Pau Escofet, Joshua Viszlai, Margaret Martonosi
abstract: Fault-tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) relies on Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes that encode logical qubits across many physical qubits to detect and correct errors. The surface code is among the most widely studied codes due to its high error threshold, the existence of efficient decoders, and hardware-friendly properties: a planar, two-dimensional layout with nearest-neighbor connectivity. In practice, however, the fabrication of solid-state quantum processors introduces hardware defects, resulting in defective qubits and couplers that must be discarded. Adapting the surface code to these defects often requires measuring the $X$- and $Z$-type checks in separate rounds rather than simultaneously. In this work, we investigate the optimal $X$-to-$Z$ checks round-scheduling ratio under biased noise systems. Our results characterize how key architectural parameters, such as noise bias, code distance, and defect rate, impact the logical error rate. We provide insights into how to determine the optimal scheduling ratio directly from device calibration data, enabling manufacturers to maximize performance without extensive simulations. Our approach reduces the logical error rate by up to $4.25\times$ at a $1\%$ defect rate and up to $8.46\times$ at a $2\%$ defect rate for a distance-$13$ surface code under moderately biased noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the benefits of round-scheduling extend beyond the defective-hardware setting. In biased-noise architectures subject to CNOT crosstalk, separating $X$ and $Z$ measurement rounds yields up to $4.5\times$ reduction in logical error rate.
summary: This paper analyzes the optimal timing ratio for performing X-type versus Z-type syndrome measurements in surface codes built on imperfect hardware. By tailoring this measurement schedule according to the underlying noise bias, the authors demonstrate substantial reductions in the logical error rate. This work provides a practical guide for quantum hardware manufacturers to maximize performance without exhaustive simulation.
main_problem: The study investigates optimizing the scheduling ratio between X-type and Z-type syndrome measurements in surface codes that are adapted to function despite hardware defects.
main_result: Optimal scheduling ratios, which depend on the noise bias, can significantly reduce the logical error rate by factors up to 8.46x compared to uniform scheduling, even when considering crosstalk effects.
method: The authors use extensive numerical simulations based on a circuit-level noise model to characterize how varying the X:Z measurement round ratio impacts the overall logical error rate (LER).
model_or_system: The physical system is the Surface Code, a leading candidate for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing. It is modeled as being implemented on hardware containing stochastic defects and operating under biased noise conditions.
key_observables: Logical Error Rate (LER), $	ext{LER}_X$, and $	ext{LER}_Z$.
important_parameters: Noise bias ($\eta = p_Z/p_X$), code distance ($d$), defect rate, and the X-to-Z scheduling ratio ($R_X:R_Z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that defects necessitate alternating X/Z measurements (Snakes and Ladders framework) and focuses on the low-to-moderate bias regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate surface code patches with varying defect rates, show components like data qubits and defective couplers, and depict decoding graphs showing interleaved X and Z super-stabilizers based on the scheduling ratio.
paper_structure: The paper systematically investigates the optimal $X$-to-$Z$ check round-scheduling ratio under biased noise for defect-adapted surface codes. It develops methods to determine this optimum from calibration data, quantifies the LER reduction achieved by optimizing the schedule, and extends these findings to crosstalk-dominated architectures.
why_interesting: While focused on QEC theory, understanding how measurement scheduling mitigates correlated errors (like those induced by defects or crosstalk) provides insights into error management in complex quantum hardware architectures relevant to AMO platforms.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. (left) Distance-5 rotated surface code with d2 data qubits and d2 −1 ancilla qubits which measure X- and Z-type stabilizers. (middle) Surface code under the presence of 1% defect rate, with a defective ancilla qubit, necessitating two super-stabilizers (one X, one Z) to obtain the syndrome. (right) Surface code under the presence of 2% defect rate, with one defective ancilla, one defective data qubit, and two defective couplers.

Fig. 2. Probability of obtaining a non-defective processor as a function of the total number of components, for hardware defect rates of 0.5%, 1% and 2%. Vertical dashed lines mark the component counts corresponding to representative code distances.

Fig. 3. (left) The X & Z decoding graph for the left patch depicted in Figure 1. Circular nodes represent bulk stabilizer nodes and diamond nodes represent boundary nodes. With no defects, both the X and the Z stabilizers are measured in every round. (right) The Z∗and X∗decoding graphs for the two alternating syndrome extraction rounds of the middle patch in Figure 1, where hatched nodes mark defective stabilizers. The non-defective X and Z stabilizers are measured in every round, while the X and Z super-stabilizers of the defective surface code are interleaved according to the scheduling ratio RX:RZ.

Fig. 4. Logical error rate for defective systems (dr = 1%) for a logical qubit prepared in the X basis (blue) and the Z basis (red), across different scheduling ratios (RX:RZ), for code distances d ∈{9, 11, 13}. The solid black line shows the average of the two bases. Under symmetric noise (top row), the optimum schedule is RX:RZ = 1:1; under Z-biased noise (bottom row), it shifts towards larger RX.

Fig. 5. Average logical error rate as a function of the scheduling ratio R, for code distances 9 and 11 in systems with increasing bias from η = 1 to η = 10 (dr = 1%). The optimum schedule moves towards larger RX:RZ as η increases, and its improvement over RX:RZ = 1:1 grows with bias.
